chunks: Humayd ibn Ziyad, from al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'a, from Ibn Ribat, and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr — both together — from Ibn Udhayna, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, that he asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him)

about a man who says to his wife: 'You are forbidden unto me', or 'a stranger', or 'cut-off', or 'disavowed', or 'free'. He said: 'All of this is nothing. The divorce is only when he says to her at the beginning of the waiting period, after she has been purified from her menstruation, before he has intercourse with her: "You are divorced" or "Begin your waiting period", intending by that the divorce — and he calls two just men as witnesses to that.'

key_terms.اعْتَدِّي: Alternative correct formula: 'Begin your waiting period'
key_terms.الْعِدَّةُ: The 'iddah — the legally mandated waiting period a woman must observe after divorce
key_terms.الْمَحِيضُ: Menstruation; purification from it is a prerequisite for pronouncing divorce
key_terms.بَائِنَةٌ: Irrevocable separation; a colloquial term sometimes used to signal divorce but lacking legal force
key_terms.بَتَّةٌ: Final severance; another informal expression sometimes used but invalid for divorce
key_terms.رَجُلَيْنِ عَدْلَيْنِ: Two just men — the required witnesses for divorce to be legally valid
key_terms.طَالِقٌ: The correct divorce formula: 'You are divorced'

ai.seo_question: What phrases count as valid divorce in Shia Islam according to Imam al-Baqir?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) clarifies that informal colloquial phrases sometimes used as expressions of divorce — such as 'You are forbidden to me,' 'a stranger,' 'cut-off,' 'disavowed,' or 'free' — carry no legal weight in Islamic law. Valid divorce (talaq) requires a specific formula ('You are divorced' or 'Begin your waiting period'), pronounced at the beginning of the wife's post-menstrual waiting period before any resumption of conjugal relations, and must be witnessed by two just men. This ruling reflects the Shia jurisprudential position that talaq requires precise conditions to be legally effective, protecting both parties from inadvertent or emotionally driven ruptures.

en.hubeali:
Humeyd Bin Ziyad, from Al Hassan Bin Muhammad Bin Sama’at, from Ibn Rabat, and Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abu Umeyr, both together, from Ibn Azina, 
(It has been narrated) from Muhammad Bin Muslim

who asked Abu Ja’far<sup>asws</sup> about a man who says to his wife, ‘You are forbidden unto me’, or ‘a stranger’, or ‘cut-off’, or ‘disavowed’, or ‘free’. He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘All these are not with anything. But rather, the divorce is that he should be saying to her in the beginning of the waiting period, after what she had been purified from her menstruation, before he copulates with her, ‘You are divorced’, or ‘Begin your waiting period’, intending the divorce by that, and there witness upon that, two just men’.
en.sarwar: 1. Humayd ibn Ziyad has narrated from al-Hassan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama‘ah from ibn Ribat and Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from ibn abu ‘Umayr all from ibn ‘Udhaynah from Muhammad ibn Muslim who has said the following: “I once asked abu Ja’far, ‘Alayhi al-Salam,

about the case of a man who says to his wife, ‘You are unlawful for me, you are stranger to me, you are cut off, you are free and your way is clear.’ He (the Imam) said, ‘All of such expressions do not have any valid effect in the form of divorce. Divorce is when one just before waiting period, after her becoming clean from Hayd (menses) without sexual intercourse says, ‘Anti Taliq (you are let go, divorced) or ’ 1‘tady (commence waiting period) intending thereby Talaq (divorce) which must be in the presence of two witnesses.’”
